children: By Peter Coy

America's wealth divide is increasingly a generational one. From 1989 to 2022, households headed by people age 65 to 74 added $231,000 to their median net worth, while households headed by people under 35 added just $20,000, according to Federal Reserve data.

There are several reasons for the widening gap. Older Americans have ridden decades of gains in stocks and real estate, while many younger people are stuck in rentals, struggling with the soaring cost of child care and the burden of student debt.

The result is that older Americans may have more capacity to give to their children and grandchildren than ever before. And many would rather give the money now, when it can help with a house, child care or other major expenses, than leave it behind after they die.

The good news for families considering such gifts: The tax code makes it easier to give money while you're alive-with "warm hands," as the saying goes-than many people realize. Here are some answers to common questions about such giving.
My understanding is that there is a $19,000 limit on annual giving per recipient. Is that right?

That is a common misunderstanding. That figure is the limit on how much you can give without submitting paperwork to the Internal Revenue Service. As of this year, you can give up to $19,000 to each of your children, each of their spouses, and each of your grandchildren, every year generally without filing any paperwork to the IRS in the form of a gift-tax return.

Those annual gifts add up. If you gave one child $19,000 a year for 30 years, you would have transferred $570,000. A married couple could give that child $38,000 a year, or $1.14 million over 30 years. They could make separate gifts of the same size to the child's spouse and to each grandchild.

And you can give considerably more than that. Gifts above the annual exclusion generally require you to file Form 709 with the IRS, but that doesn't mean you owe tax. Instead, the excess counts against your lifetime gift-and-estate-tax exemption, which in 2026 is $15 million per person, or potentially $30 million for a married couple.

Say you give your daughter $100,000 this year. The first $19,000 falls under the annual exclusion. The remaining $81,000 counts against your $15 million lifetime exemption. You would file a gift-tax return, but in most cases you wouldn't owe any gift tax.
In other words, the federal gift tax simply isn't an issue for most families-even families making quite substantial gifts.
Sounds like I won't need to worry about Form 709.

Filing is still worth doing even if you're sure you will never owe anything. Once a gift is adequately disclosed on Form 709, assuming no fraud is involved, the IRS generally has only three years to challenge how it was reported. If it isn't disclosed on a return, that three-year clock never starts, and the IRS can potentially question the gift years later.
What's more, your children's mortgage lenders might want documentation that a down-payment contribution from you was a gift, not a loan. The form creates that paper trail.
My friend paid directly for his grandchildren's tuition. Does that count toward the limits you just described?

No. Tuition payments made directly to a qualifying school, and qualifying medical expenses paid directly to the provider, are entirely excluded from gift tax, with no dollar cap. They don't count against either the $19,000 annual exclusion or your lifetime exemption. Note that the education exclusion covers tuition only-not room, board, books or supplies.
What about "529" education-savings plans?

Grandparents love to contribute to 529 plans. And there is a front-loading option that most people don't know about. The IRS lets you contribute five years' worth of annual exclusions at once-namely, up to $95,000 per beneficiary in 2026, or $190,000 from a married couple. The money starts compounding immediately instead of trickling in over the five years. But you have to file Form 709 to make that election, and the contribution generally uses up your annual gift-tax exclusion for that beneficiary during those five years.

One newer wrinkle: As of 2024, under the Secure 2.0 law, if a 529 has money left over after a beneficiary finishes school, up to $35,000 lifetime can be rolled into a Roth IRA for that beneficiary. That reduces use-it-or-lose-it anxiety. (The rollover counts toward the beneficiary's annual Roth IRA contribution limit, which is $7,500 for 2026. Only money that's been in the account at least five years can be rolled over. The beneficiary must have earned income in the rollover year at least equal to the amount of the rollover, and the account must have been open for at least 15 years.)

I was always told that the best way to minimize taxes is to leave appreciated stocks in my estate, so my children inherit them on a "step-up" basis-that is, they won't owe capital-gains tax on the appreciation of the shares that occurred before they inherited them.

The step-up in cost basis can be extremely valuable. If you give appreciated stock to your children during your lifetime, they generally inherit your cost basis, meaning they could face a big capital-gains tax if they choose to sell. If they inherit the stock at your death, however, the basis generally resets to its market value at that time, potentially eliminating capital-gains tax on all the appreciation that occurred during your lifetime.

On the other hand, if your children or grandchildren have relatively little taxable income, they may be in a low or even zero tax bracket for capital gains. So you could give them assets now, and they could turn around and sell the assets without incurring much if anything in taxes. The tax advantages of keeping your money until you die are often overstated.
How do the new Trump Accounts change the picture?

Trump Accounts went live on July 4 and are still being sorted out by the IRS. The short version: Money grows in them tax-deferred. Parents can contribute up to $5,000 of after-tax money per year per child under 18, and employers can kick in up to $2,500. Grandparents can contribute too, but the $5,000 annual cap is shared across all contributors combined.

Because the child cannot touch the money until age 18, contributions would ordinarily not qualify for the annual $19,000 exclusion, so donors would have to file a Form 709. But the IRS doesn't want to be deluged with those forms, so it has come up with a safe harbor that will relieve most taxpayers of the need to submit the 709, says Lawrence Pon, a certified financial planner in Redwood City, Calif. Getting professional help with the paperwork, if you're in doubt, is probably wise.

One drawback of the Trump Accounts is that 18-year-olds who gain control of the accounts may not handle the windfall responsibly. (And any withdrawals they make are taxable at ordinary income-tax rates, for what it's worth.) A 529, by contrast, stays under the parent's control.
So you're saying I should give away all my money?

Not at all. A gift is irrevocable, and your own retirement expenses aren't. The tax code doesn't ask whether you can afford to give-that is a separate question you have to answer for yourself, and it should come before any tax optimization.

If Medicaid for long-term care is a realistic near-term possibility, be careful: If you make gifts less than five years before applying, Medicaid may assume that you're trying to impoverish yourself to qualify for the government benefit, and deem you ineligible for Medicaid for a penalty period.
